frontier.hypothesis: The reuse-p chassis D1 (W1 + loop 2's base addend reusing the carried pointer `p`), which is 5 at 126 insns with ONLY loop 2's preheader copy missing, is one clause-B consumer away from 127 — and unlike V1 it needs no addend RELOAD, so the consumer no longer has to pay for a load target does not have. The untested consumer class is a later-EBB use of `p` that is neither a loop-2 body address (E-s21-1: always re-expressed as base + constant) nor a post-loop pointer derivation (E-s21-3: always deletes a reload) — specifically, a use of `p` in the loop-2 EXIT block that is a VALUE use rather than an address base, e.g. the `(slot_a << 16) | slot_b` / arg1 / dist stores' address chain rewritten so that `link` is derived from a pointer expression that keeps `p` live without replacing a ctx+0x10 read.
frontier.mechanism: E-s20-1 as sharpened by E-s21-4: a preheader copy exists iff the copy's DESTINATION has a use in a later EBB. D1 already satisfies every other condition — the base add survives (E-s20-2), the addend is not reloaded, and the preheader is otherwise byte-correct at 126. The remaining question is purely whether any later-EBB use of the destination exists whose materialised instruction does not simultaneously delete one of target's reloads (E-s21-3's uniform failure mode) or get re-canonicalised to `base` (E-s21-1's).
frontier.next_probe: On D1, sweep clause-B consumers that touch ctx+0x10-based state rather than ctx+0xC-based state, so no ctx+0xC reload can be deleted: (a) derive `link` as `*(u8 **)(ctx + 0x10) + (*(s16 *)(ctx + 0x6) << 4)` but guard-order it after a statement that reads `p`; (b) write the `*(s32 *)(link + 0x4) = (slot_a << 16) | slot_b;` store through an address expression that mentions `p` only in a subexpression that cancels; (c) use `p` as the base of the FIRST record update (`rec_a`) but with the shift recomputed so the addend is not the deleted reload's value — E2 measured the naive form at 31, so vary the shift/association rather than repeating it. Score every cell with sandbox --disable all and record build_insns; any cell at 127 gets an objdump-normalised residual diff, and any cell whose loop-2 preheader emits `addu DST,SRC,zero` BEFORE the base add is the win even if its own score is above 3.

frontier.hypothesis: D3's preheader has target's two instruction KINDS in the wrong order (`addu a0,a1,a0 / addu a1,a0,zero` vs `addu a3,a0,zero / addu a0,a1,a3`). The order is decided by which pseudo local-alloc's optimize_reg_copy_1 rewrites — s15 (1) established that pass re-points the base add onto the copy when the copy is orphaned, and D3's copy is NOT orphaned (its use is the body limit read). Removing that use while keeping the copy would flip the order; the only way to do so is to make the copy's use one that combine folds into an instruction that already exists.
frontier.mechanism: s15 (1): optimize_reg_copy_1 (local-alloc.c:700, dispatched :1006) rewrites SRC to DEST over the range where SRC dies, producing target's `copy then base-add-reading-the-copy` order, and nothing after local-alloc runs DCE. s16 (2): whether cse leaves the ORIGINAL or the COPY at the base add is the single decision that decides the order. D3 is the first cell where both instructions exist, so the order question is now isolated from the existence question.
frontier.next_probe: Take D3 and vary ONLY what the body limit use looks like, holding the reuse-p base fixed: (a) limit read via `p` with the offset split (`*(s32 *)((s32)p + (sh2 + 0x20))`), (b) limit read via a second named local initialised from `p` in the preheader, (c) limit read via `p` but with loop 2 written as a `while` with the test duplicated rather than a `do/while`. Then dump `.cse` and `.lreg` for the best cell with `pwsh tools/grinder/dump.ps1 func_80017848` (instrumented cc1 is tools/gcc-2.7.2/cc1, never build/cc1; re-prove codegen identity on the whole TU first) and read whether the base add reads the original or the copy at insn 162/168 — that single RTL fact predicts the order for every future cell without another sandbox sweep.

frontier.hypothesis: Loop 1 and loop 2 may not need INDEPENDENT clause-B purchases. This body pays for loop 1 with `p = q;` (one point, landing where target has `lw a0,12(s2)`) and cannot pay for loop 2 at all; D1 pays for loop 2's base add for free but has no consumer. A chassis where loop 1's copy destination and loop 2's carried pointer are the SAME name, with the single `p = q;`-equivalent statement serving as the later-EBB consumer for loop 1's copy AND the source of loop 2's reuse-p addend, has never been built — every prior cell either deleted the tail (B1/B2, 125) or kept it with a FRESH loop-2 read (V1, 3).
frontier.mechanism: E-s21-4 pins that the consumer must read the copy's DESTINATION. In V1 the destination is `q` and the consumer is `p = q;`. D1 replaces loop 2's fresh read with the carried `p` — which is the VALUE of that very consumer. So the consumer statement is already doing double duty in D1's ancestor; what has not been tried is making loop 2's addend be `q` (the loop-1 copy destination) directly while KEEPING `p = q;` for definedness on the skip path, so loop 2's base add reads the destination and thereby extends the copy's live range past the join.
frontier.next_probe: Build D1' = W1 + `p = q;` tail retained + loop 2's guard two-step and base addend both reading `q` rather than `p`, with `q` pre-initialised (e.g. `q = *(u8 **)(ctx + 0xC);` at the top, immediately before loop 1's guard) so it is defined when loop 1 is skipped — note this differs from B2, which read `q` at the guard but DELETED the tail and therefore lost the destination use. Then the three obvious variants: tail written as `p = q;` vs `p = *(u8 **)(ctx + 0xC);` vs no `p` at all; and loop 2's limit read via `q` vs via `base`. Score with sandbox --disable all, record build_insns, and diff any cell at 126 or 127.
